title: FDA Approves Two New Cholesterol Drugs, Including First-Ever Oral PCSK9 Pill
excerpt: A once-monthly injectable and a daily pill give patients new options to fight high cholesterol, a condition that disproportionately affects South Asians.
body:
• Merck's Lipfendra (enlicitide), approved July 16, 2026, is the first oral PCSK9 inhibitor — a daily pill that lowered LDL cholesterol by 56% in clinical trials.
  • LIB Therapeutics' Lerochol (lerodalcibep), approved December 2025, is a once-monthly injectable stable at room temperature for up to three months.
  • Both drugs expand treatment options beyond existing PCSK9 injectables like Amgen's Repatha and Regeneron's Praluent.
  • South Asians face 50–60% higher cardiovascular risk, making new cholesterol-lowering therapies especially relevant for Indian diaspora communities.

The FDA has approved two new cholesterol-lowering drugs in the PCSK9 inhibitor class within seven months of each other, giving doctors and patients a wider toolkit to manage a condition that remains the leading cause of cardiovascular death worldwide.

A Pill Instead of a Needle

Merck's Lipfendra (enlicitide), approved on July 16, 2026, is the first PCSK9 inhibitor available as an oral pill. Taken once daily at 20 milligrams, it eliminates the need for injections that have limited uptake of existing PCSK9 drugs despite their proven effectiveness.

In the CORALreef Lipids trial involving 2,904 patients already on statins, Lipfendra reduced LDL cholesterol — the so-called "bad" cholesterol — by 56% compared to placebo after 24 weeks. Merck has set a list price of $10.50 per day.

"This is a pivotal moment as we bring the first U.S. FDA-approved oral PCSK9 inhibitor to adults with high LDL-C, offering patients an important new option."

— Dean Y. Li, President of Merck Research Laboratories

Scotiabank analyst Louise Chen has estimated Lipfendra could reach "peak sales potential of tens of billions of dollars," reflecting the vast population of patients who struggle to hit cholesterol targets with statins alone.

A More Convenient Monthly Injection

LIB Therapeutics' Lerochol (lerodalcibep-liga), approved in December 2025 and expected to be commercially available by spring 2026, takes a different approach. It is a third-generation PCSK9 inhibitor delivered as a once-monthly, self-administered subcutaneous injection. The drug is stable at room temperature for up to three months, a practical advantage over existing injectables that often require refrigeration.

In clinical trials under the LIBerate program, lerodalcibep delivered sustained LDL-C reductions of 50% or more.

"Lerochol was designed for patients who need lifelong treatment to achieve and maintain the new lower LDL-C goals, especially those with cardiovascular disease and the millions with inherited high cholesterol."

— Evan Stein, MD, PhD, Founder and CEO, LIB Therapeutics

Why This Matters for South Asians

About one in four American adults has elevated LDL cholesterol, according to the American Heart Association. But the stakes are sharper for people of South Asian descent, who face significantly higher rates of coronary artery disease at younger ages — a disparity linked to genetic, metabolic, and dietary factors. Studies consistently show South Asians have a 50 to 60 percent greater risk of cardiovascular disease compared to the general population.

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans, many of whom have a family history of heart disease, a daily cholesterol pill that does not require injections could lower a practical barrier to treatment adherence.

The Competitive Landscape

The PCSK9 inhibitor market has been dominated by injectable biologics — Amgen's Repatha and Regeneron/Sanofi's Praluent — which are effective but have faced limited adoption due to cost, the inconvenience of injections, and the need for cold storage. Both Lipfendra and Lerochol address these barriers in different ways: one by eliminating injections entirely, the other by making them less frequent and easier to store.

Familial hypercholesterolemia, the inherited form of high cholesterol that both drugs are approved to treat, affects roughly 1 in 200 people globally. Left untreated, it can lead to premature heart attacks and cardiovascular death.

What's Next

Merck's Lipfendra is expected to become commercially available in the coming months. Physicians will likely weigh factors including insurance coverage, patient preference, and the severity of cholesterol elevation when choosing between the oral and injectable options. Both drugs are approved for use alongside diet, exercise, and existing statin therapy.
